blocks.text: Development is conventionally assessed in **four major domains**:

subsections.subsection_title: 2. The golden rule of developmental assessment

blocks.text: **What can the child do independently, consistently and appropriately for age?**
**Ask the caregiver AND demonstrate/test the skill yourself.**
“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I'd like to assess your child's development by asking you some questions and doing a few simple activities with your child. Is that okay?”

blocks.title: Developmental assessment should ideally be performed when the child is:

items.text: In an environment where they can move freely

blocks.text: A sick, tired or frightened child may perform below their true developmental level.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Start by determining the child's age

blocks.text: “What is the child's date of birth?”
You cannot interpret a child's ability without knowing their age.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Ask the parent an open question first

blocks.text: A very good OSCE opening is:
“What can your child do now that you feel is appropriate for their age?”
“Is there anything about your child's development that concerns you?”
This gives you the parent's perspective before you begin your formal assessment.
Gross motor development involves large muscle groups and posture.
“When did your child start holding their head steadily?”
“When did they start sitting without support?”
These are approximate developmental milestones; individual children vary.

rows: Sits with support / may begin sitting briefly
Pulls to stand / crawls or moves around
Runs well, walks up stairs with support

blocks.text: Don't treat these as rigid deadlines.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. How to assess gross motor development in an OSCE

blocks.text: Don't simply ask the mother whether the child can run.
“I'd like to see the child walk and run if possible.”

items.text: Ability to rise from the floor

blocks.text: “Can they transfer objects from one hand to another?”

rows: Mature pincer grasp; releases objects intentionally
Copies a circle approximately; uses utensils
Copies simple shapes; draws a person with several parts
Copies more complex shapes; improved handwriting

blocks.text: Give the child an age-appropriate object.

items.text: Does the child look at it?

blocks.text: This is more than simply asking whether the child talks.
How the child uses communication to interact.

rows: Uses short sentences; speech increasingly understandable
Speaks in sentences; asks many questions

blocks.text: Ask the child to name it.

subsections.subsection_title: 17. What should you observe during the station?

blocks.text: Even before testing milestones, watch the child.
Does the child turn when called?
These observations are particularly important when considering **autism spectrum disorder**.
This is a useful examiner question.
A structured tool used to identify children who may require further assessment.

blocks.title: A more comprehensive evaluation to determine:

blocks.text: You should know these very well.

items.text: Failure to sit/walk within expected developmental range
No meaningful communication by an age when it should be emerging
Significant lack of response to language

blocks.text: A child previously spoke 20 words but subsequently stops speaking.
“Has your child ever been able to do something that they can no longer do?”
“Were there any illnesses, seizures or other events around that time?”
**Regression is a red flag requiring further evaluation.**
Developmental delay means the child acquires developmental skills later than expected.
A child with isolated speech delay:

Gross motor — normal
Fine motor — normal
Social — normal
Language — delayed
This is different from a child delayed in all domains.
A commonly used clinical definition is significant delay in **two or more developmental domains** in a young child.
Global developmental delay is a **description**, not an underlying diagnosis.
You need to investigate the cause.
If developmental delay is accompanied by abnormal movement or tone, assess for cerebral palsy.
This can be tested as a communication or developmental OSCE.
Don't diagnose autism from one observation.
Observe whether the child follows your gaze/point.
“Does your child point to things to show you something interesting?”
“Does your child bring toys to show you?”
“Does your child respond when you call their name?”
“Have they lost any previously acquired skills?”
**Summarize and recommend further assessment if abnormal**

“This is a 2-year-old child. The child is alert and appropriately interactive with good eye contact and response to the examiner. Gross motor development is appropriate, as the child walks and runs independently. Fine motor skills are appropriate, with the child able to manipulate objects and scribble. Language development is appropriate for age, with use of two-word phrases and understanding of simple commands. Social development is appropriate, with appropriate interaction and imitation. There is no reported history of developmental regression.”

subsections.subsection_title: 28. How to present an abnormal assessment

blocks.text: “This is a 3-year-old child with significant delay in expressive and receptive language, while gross and fine motor development appear relatively preserved. There is also reduced eye contact and limited social interaction. There is a history of loss of previously acquired words. These findings raise concern for a neurodevelopmental disorder, and the child requires comprehensive developmental assessment, including hearing assessment and appropriate specialist evaluation.”
Notice that you don't jump straight to:
You describe your findings first and then give the clinical impression.

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are the four major developmental domains?

blocks.text: Gross motor, fine motor, language/communication, and social/personal development.
Loss of previously acquired developmental skills.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. Why is developmental regression important?

blocks.text: It is a red flag that may indicate neurological, metabolic, genetic or other significant pathology and requires further assessment.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What is global developmental delay?

blocks.text: Significant delay affecting two or more developmental domains in a young child.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What is the difference between receptive and expressive language?

blocks.text: Receptive language refers to understanding language, while expressive language refers to producing language or communicating.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What would make you suspect autism?

blocks.text: Difficulties with social communication and interaction, such as poor eye contact, poor response to name and impaired joint attention, together with restricted or repetitive behaviours or interests.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What else should you assess in a child with developmental delay?

blocks.text: Hearing, vision, neurological status, growth, nutrition, birth and perinatal history, family history and relevant investigations depending on the clinical presentation.
You should **observe and interact with the child**.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ Treating milestone ages as exact deadlines

blocks.text: Use milestones as **approximate expected periods**, not rigid dates.
**“Has the child lost any skills they previously had?”**
A child who appears to have language delay may have **hearing impairment**.
A frightened child may not demonstrate their true abilities.
You need a broader assessment of social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours.
When you walk into the station, think:
**A → O → G → F → L → S → R**

**A** — Age
**O** — Observe
**G** — Gross motor
**F** — Fine motor
**L** — Language
**S** — Social
**R** — Regression
Rather than trying to memorize every milestone at once, anchor yourself around these:
Sits independently, transfers objects, babbles, stranger anxiety.
Pulls to stand/cruises, may walk, pincer grasp, first words.
Walks/runs, scribbles, increasing vocabulary, follows simple commands.
Runs well, two-word phrases, builds/plays, increasing independence.
More complex sentences, interactive play, climbs/jumps.
Hops, draws simple figures/shapes, imaginative/cooperative play.
Skips, improved fine motor control, more complex language and social interaction.
